title: Public investment (capital budgets)
headline: £134bn in 2029-30. Adds to debt, not to the day-to-day budget.
description: Change total departmental capital budgets from April 2027, as a percentage of the OBR's forecast (£132.8bn in 2027-28, £134.2bn in 2029-30). Investment adds to borrowing and to net financial liabilities but not to the current budget, so it tests the investment rule rather than the stability rule. A 1% change is about £1.3bn a year.

baselinePolicy.text: Capital DEL of £122.5bn in 2026-27 rising to £134.2bn in 2029-30 and £138.1bn in 2030-31, after the OBR's underspend assumptions of £9.7bn in 2026-27 and about £3.7bn a year in the final three years of the Spending Review period.
alreadyIncludes: Spending Review 2025 capital settlements to 2029-30, including defence capital rising from £23.2bn to £33.2bn (Table 5.4).
Total capital spending assumed at £138bn in 2030-31, implying real growth of 0.8% in that year (EFO paragraph 4.14).

caveats: Applied to the OBR's capital DEL forecast, which already nets off its underspend assumption; a change is assumed to be spent in full.

Every pound is treated as public sector net investment: depreciation on new assets and any financial-transaction element (loans and equity, which affect net financial liabilities differently) are not modelled.

considerations.text: Part of capital DEL is financial transactions such as loans and equity: the Spending Review tables strip out £8.8bn in 2029-30 to give capital DEL excluding financial transactions of £143.1bn against a total of £151.9bn. Financial transactions add to borrowing measures but are matched by an asset in net financial liabilities, so the effect of a change on the investment rule depends on its mix.

Departments have historically underspent capital budgets; the OBR assumes £9.7bn of underspending in 2026-27 and about £3.7bn a year after that, and notes that in 2025-26 departments surrendered only 0.2% of capital budgets against a post-pandemic average closer to 5%. Extra capital budgets may not all be spent when planned.
Any effect of public investment on the economy's capacity, and so on receipts, is not modelled here; the OBR's forecast is not re-run when you change the lever.
